subject: biology
title: Gene mutations
key_idea: A gene mutation is a change in the sequence of base pairs in DNA. Substitution, insertion and deletion can change the amino acids in a polypeptide. An insertion or deletion usually shifts the reading frame and has a bigger effect than a substitution.

blocks.text: A gene mutation changes the base sequence of a gene. This section covers how mutations arise.

items: A **gene mutation** is a change in the sequence of base pairs in a DNA molecule. It may result in an altered polypeptide.
Mutations can arise spontaneously during DNA replication, when a wrong base is paired.
The mutation rate is increased by **mutagenic agents** (mutagens), such as ionising radiation, ultraviolet light and some chemicals.
Mutation changes the genetic diversity of a population.
A gene mutation is a change in base sequence.
Mutations occur spontaneously, mostly in replication, and mutagens increase their rate.

blocks.text: Mutations are named by what happens to the bases.

rows: One base is replaced by another
One or more bases are added
A frame shift if the number is not a multiple of three
One or more bases are lost
A frame shift if the number is not a multiple of three
A sequence of bases is reversed
Changes the triplets within that sequence
A sequence of bases is repeated
Adds extra triplets or shifts the frame
A sequence of bases moves to a different position in the DNA
Changes where the sequence is read, so genes may be disrupted

items: Only one triplet is changed, so at most one amino acid changes.
A **silent** mutation gives a different triplet for the same amino acid, because the code is degenerate. The polypeptide is unchanged.
A **missense** mutation changes one amino acid. The effect depends on where it is.
A **nonsense** mutation turns an amino acid triplet into a stop triplet, which shortens the polypeptide.
Adding or removing a base changes every triplet after it, because the code is non-overlapping and read in threes. This is a **frame shift**.
Every amino acid downstream of the mutation can change, so the polypeptide is usually very different.
Inserting or deleting three bases in a row, or a multiple of three, adds or removes amino acids but keeps the frame the same for the rest of the gene.

diagram.alt: Choose a type of mutation and see the effect on the polypeptide.
diagram.prompt: Pick a mutation to a gene whose mRNA reads AAA GCC UUU GGG

options.label: Substitution: AAA to AAG
results: No change: both triplets code for the same amino acid (silent)

options.label: Substitution: GCC to GAC
results: One amino acid is different (missense). The rest is unchanged

options.label: Deletion of the first A
results: Frame shift: every triplet after the mutation is changed
options.explanation: The bases are read in threes from the start.

options.label: Insertion of a G after the first triplet
results: Frame shift: every triplet after the insertion is changed
options.explanation: One extra base moves every later triplet along by one.

items: Substitution changes one triplet; because the code is degenerate it may change nothing.
Insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three causes a frame shift.
A frame shift usually has a bigger effect than a substitution.

sections.heading: Effects on protein structure and function

blocks.text: A mutation matters only if it changes the polypeptide. This section links base changes to protein function.

items.text: A different base or number of bases changes the mRNA codons.
Different amino acids may be joined, so the primary structure changes.
Different R groups form different hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds, so the tertiary structure changes.
The shape of an enzyme's active site or another binding site changes, so the protein may no longer work.

items: A **harmful** mutation stops the protein working, as in cystic fibrosis, where the CFTR protein is faulty.
A **neutral** mutation has no effect on the phenotype, for example a silent substitution.
A **beneficial** mutation gives the organism an advantage, such as an enzyme that works better or a new allele that gives resistance to a disease. It may then be selected for.

blocks.text: Meiosis also produces variation, which is covered in another note.

items: Mutation changes the base sequence, then the amino acid sequence, then the protein's shape and function.
The effect can be harmful, neutral or beneficial.

checks.q: Explain why a substitution mutation does not always change the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
checks.a: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet. A substitution may produce a new triplet that codes for the same amino acid, so the polypeptide is unchanged.

checks.q: Explain why the deletion of a single base usually has a greater effect on a polypeptide than a substitution.
checks.a: Deleting a base causes a frame shift. Every triplet after the deletion is read differently, so many amino acids change. A substitution changes only one triplet and so at most one amino acid.

checks.q: Describe how a change in the base sequence of a gene could stop an enzyme working.
checks.a: The mRNA codons change, so a different amino acid sequence (primary structure) is made. Different R groups form different bonds, so the tertiary structure and active site shape change. The substrate can no longer bind to form enzyme–substrate complexes.

items: Gene mutations include addition, deletion, substitution, inversion, duplication and translocation of bases.
Gene mutations occur spontaneously, and mutagenic agents increase the rate.
Be able to relate the nature of a gene mutation to its effect on the encoded polypeptide, including whether the mutation changes only one triplet or causes a frame shift for all downstream triplets.
Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations.
Cystic fibrosis results from one of a number of possible mutations in the gene for the CFTR protein, a channel for chloride ions in the cell surface membrane.
The most common mutation is a deletion of three bases, which removes one amino acid. The protein folds incorrectly and does not reach the membrane.
Other mutations are substitutions, insertions and deletions at different places in the same gene. Different mutations give different effects.
Outline how substitution, deletion and insertion of nucleotides may each affect the polypeptide.
A substitution may be silent, cause one amino acid to change or create a stop codon.
A deletion or insertion of a nucleotide changes the reading frame, so the amino acids after it are different.
Substitution, insertion or deletion of one or more nucleotides, and the possible effects.
Effects on protein production and function may be beneficial, neutral or harmful. Give an example of each, with a reason.
